Mahmudul Islam, Senior Advocate, instructed by Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record--For the Appellant. 

Shafiq Ahmed, Senior Advocate (Tabarak Hossain, Advocate with him) instructed by AKM Shahidul Huq, Advocate-on-Record---For the Respondent No. 1. 

Respondent Nos. 2-6---Not Represented.
parties:
Ruhul Amin ------ Appellant
vs
Official Liquidator, Mahaluxmi Bank Ltd ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
10. The High Court Division also found that the defendant No. 1 claimed that most of the land settled in favour of Aparna Charan, his father, were in RS Jote No. 81 but some part thereof was recorded wrongly in the name of Sarada Kripa Lala in RS Jote No. 86 and after coming to know about the same from the defendant No. 2 for the first time in the year 1954 he filed JM Case No. 230 of 1954-55 but the above claim is not correct as there is no corroboration from any witness in this regard and the fact that Aparna Charan did not take settlement of the full CS Plot No. 1748 and took settlement of a part of it is evident from Exhibit F, i.e. the order sheet of Miscellaneous Case No. 284 of 1907-08 for settlement, Exhibit G i.e. the list of tenants, Exhibit H i.e. the kabuliyat executed by Aparna Charan, Exhibit S(6) i.e. sale deed dated 26-7-1939 executed on behalf of the defendant No. 1 in favour of Jibendra Lal Dutta and Exhibit S(7) i.e. the sale deed dated 5-8-1942 executed by Jibendra Lal Dutta in favour of the defendant No. 1 which will show that the Aparna Charan entered into possession of the full CS Plot No. 1748 after demarcation of boundaries in the year 1912 and then, as will be evident from Exhibits A-A4, he retreated to the settled portion of CS Plot No. 1748 at the time of RS operation and was not in possession of RS Plot No. 2956 at the time of preparation of RS records as is evidenced by Exhibit E(1), the RS Khatian No. 776, and that is why RS Plot No. 2956 was recorded in the name of Sarada Kripa Lala who actually possessed the suit property at the time of RS operation and the defendant No. 1 has failed to rebut the presumption of RS records by any documentary or unimpeachable oral evidence and as has been held in the case of Alimuddin Munshi vs Mainuddin Talukder, 14 DLR 725, merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entries in the record of rights, the presumption under the entry is not rebutted and there must be further evidence to show that the entries are incorrect and the defendant No. 1 having failed to produce any documentary evidence or any convincing evidence to show that and further the non-payment of rent by the defendant No. 1 for RS Plot No. 2956 from 1930 to 1955 was not an inadvertence as has been urged and, on the other hand, such non payment supports that the defendant No. 1 and his predecessor had no interest in the suit property and that is why they did not pay rent for the suit property after the RS operation and further from 1930 to 1955 the defendant No. 1 and his predecessor were quite happy and content with the recording of the land settled in favour of Aparna Charan in RS Jote No. 81 and Aparna Charan paid rent for that jote in the justified belief that all the settled lands of Aparna Charan were included in it and several transactions were made in respect of the lands of Jote No. 81 with the clear understanding and belief that those dealings were in respect of the entire settled lands of Aparna Charan and the defendant No. 1 took certified copies of his father's settlement papers, Exhibits F-H in the year 1954 and he failed to show any other certified copy taken before 1954 and further, taking advantage of the moribund condition of the bank in the year 1954, the defendant No. 1 went into possession of the suit property in the year 1955 and showing interpolated Exhibits F-H obtained mutation of the suit property in his own name and started the brick field during Pakistan period as unwittingly given out by DWs 1 and 2 and then he paid rent for RS Jote No. 86 from 1955 onwards and sold 1.20 acres of the suit land to Pakistan Tobacco Co Ltd in the year 1956 and in the year 1965 he stopped manufacturing bricks and on dividing the suit property into many plots started selling those to willing purchasers till an order of status quo was passed by the High Court Division and while the bank has been able to prove that it had possession of the suit land from 1934-55 by documentary evidence and, on the other hand, the defendant No. 1 has no documentary evidence and/or any reliable oral evidence in support of his title and possession of the suit land from 1930-55 and as has been held in the case of Keshav Raghunath Deshpande vs Govind Chimnaji Deshpande, AIR 1928 Bom 287 the fact that a stranger in the present case, the bank takes possession of a property under a mistake common to all does not make his possession any less adverse and it has also been held in a number of cases, namely, Govinda vs Mallayya, 311 C 678, Kunwar Sen vs Darbarilal ILR 38 All 411, Ram Piari vs Budhsen ILR 43 All 164, Priya Sakhi vs Manbodh Bibi, ILR 44 Cal 425, that a mortgagee, who does not enter possession in his character as mortgagee, may by 12 years' adverse possession, acquire a good title against a mortgagor and in a number of cases, namely, Zaibunnessa vs Parichit, 23, IC 611, Mula Singh vs Budh Singh, 25 IC 616, and Bhari vs Abbayanath, 41, IC 862, it has also been held that a mortgagee may by 12 years' adverse possession, acquire a good title to other land of the mortgagor which had not been validly mortgaged to him and that in the present case adverse possession of the bank against Sarada Kripa Lala and his successor started from the date of mutation on 7-11-36 and the bank continued in possession and its possession stood reconfirmed during the requisition and derequisition proceedings in 1942 and 1946-47 and that in the year 1942 the defendant No. 1 re-purchased RS Jote No. 81 being fully satisfied that this was the entire settled land of his father and further, the defendant No. 1 or Sarada Kripa Lala was no where in the picture during the requisition and de-requisition proceedings and therefore taking the date of the possession of the bank to be 7-11-36, the bank acquired good title to the suit land by adverse possession and so Madhabi Lata Lala had no saleable interest in the suit land on 29-9-58 and though Mr Mahmudul Islam, relying on the case of Sarat Chandra Maiti vs Bibhaboti Debi AIR 1921 Calcutta 584, submitted that when a property is requisitioned it passes into legal custody and during the continuance of requisition such custody is for the benefit of the true owner but the above cited case is a case of attachment under section 146, CrPC and there is nothing to show that such an order of attachment under section 146, CrPC is applicable in the case of mortgage. 

 12. Leave was granted on the submissions that the defendant No. 1 transferred the major portion of the suit property to others long before the institution of the instant suit and those transferees having not been impleaded inspite of objection taken and, as such, the suit is bad for defect of parties and the High Court Division, upon an erroneous view, held that since those transferees will stand or fall with the defendant No. 1; the learned Single Judge having found that the bank was not a mortgagee in respect of the suit property and that the suit land was wrongly mutated in the name of the bank as a mortgagee in JM Case No. 236 of 1936-37 and that "the actual mutation as a mortgagee in possession does not also reflect the correct position" and there having been absolutely no oral evidence of possession by the bank, committed grave error of law in finding title of the bank by adverse possession on the basis of the order of mutation of the suit property in the above JM Case No. 236 of 1936-37 specially when in their pleading the bank did not plead that they acquired title adverse possession; there having been no evidence whatsoever of the bank's entering into possession of the suit property the learned Single Judge was manifestly wrong in holding that the correct position was that the bank entered into possession of the suit property mistakenly as a mortgagee and such a finding is solely based on surmise and conjecture; even if it is assumed for argument's sake, without however conceding that the plaintiff bank entered into possession of the suit property in the year 1936, the learned Single Judge failed to notice that the bank claiming to have entered in possession as a mortgagee and having neither pleaded nor adduced evidence to show from when the plaintiff asserted absolute title to the disputed land;, the defendant No. 1 having examined a number of person to prove his possession in the suit property and there having been no evidence adduced by either the bank or defendant No. 2 in support of this adverse possession, the learned Single Judge ought to have held that the defendant No. 1, all through, had been in possession of the suit property; the learned Single Judge misread Exhibit 5, the certified copy of the proceedings of Land Acquisition of LA Case No. 62 of 1942-43 to find possession of the bank, inasmuch as Exhibit 5 neither shows that possession of the suit property was taken from the bank nor shows that the said property was redelivered to the bank upon de-requisition and even if it is assumed for argument's sake without however conceding that the bank was in possession of the suit property prior to 30-11-1942, when the government took possession of the same the bank being a trespasser could not tack the period between 30-11-1942 and 38-1-1947 for acquisition of title by adverse possession, inasmuch as the government having taken over possession of the suit property under the law, the possession of the bank was snapped and fresh period of limitation would start to run from the time the suit property was derequisitioned and vacated by the government, Exhibit A series, i.e. the proceedings of Boundary Demarcation Miscellaneous Case No. 288 of 1911-12 and Exhibit N, the rent receipt taken together with other documents clearly establish that Aparna Charan, the father of the defendant No. 1, took settlement of the entire CS Plot No. 1748 of which the suit property was a part and he possessed the same until his death in the year 1929, before RS operation, and the learned Single Judge upon untenable ground disbelieved the case of the defendant No. 1 claiming title to the entire CS Plot No. 1748 including the suit property and failed to consider that the documents produced by him and particularly, the records of Exhibit A series and the map prepared by the Amin therein, clearly established the claim of the defendant No. 1 and also shows that the entry of the name of Sarada Kripa Lala in the RS record of rights is completely without basis, the learned Single Judge on the basis of Report of JM Case No. 230A/ 11 of 1954-55, having found Exhibit R(1), that the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit property in 1955 and the defendant No. 1 adduced oral evidence in support of his possession, whereas there having been no evidence as to how the bank came into possession of the suit property, ought to have held that the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit property ever since it was derequisitioned in 1947; the present proceeding being for recovery of possession the burden of proof was on the bank, the plaintiff to, prove its possession and the bank having failed to adduce any evidence in this regard the defendant No. 1 was not required to adduce any evidence of possession and, in this state of affairs, when the preponderance of evidence regarding possession was heavily in favour of the defendant No. 1, the learned Single Judge ignoring the preponderance of evidence wrongly found that the defendant No. 1 was not in possession of the suit property prior to 1955; the finding of the learned Single Judge that Aparna Charan did not take settlement of the entire CS plot No. 1748 and that Sarada Kripa Lala was in possession of the suit property at the time of RS operation and that the defendant No. 1 failed to rebut the presumption of the RS record of rights and the defendant No. 1 went into possession of the suit property taking advantage of the moribund condition of the bank are all contrary to the evidence on record and are the result of surmise and conjecture. 

 45. Further, Exhibit A series, i.e. the proceedings of Boundary Demarcation Miscellaneous Case No. 288 of 1911-12 and Exhibit N, the rent receipt, taken together with other documents established that Aparna Charan, the father of the defendant No. 1, took settlement of the entire CS Plot No. 1748 of which the suit property was a part and he possessed the same until his death in the year 1929, before RS operation and the learned Single Judge upon untenable ground disbelieved the case of the defendant No. 1 claiming title to the entire CS Plot No. 1748 including the suit property. The learned Single Judge also failed to consider that the documents produced by the defendant No. 1, particularly the records of Exhibit A series and the map prepared by the Amin therein, clearly established the claim of the defendant No. 1 in the suit property and also show that the entry of the name of Sarada Kripa Lala in the RS record of rights is completely without basis. The learned Single Judge on the basis of Report of JM Case No. 230A/ 11 of 1954-55, having found Exhibit R(1), that the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit property in the year 1955 and the defendant No. 1 adduced oral evidence in support of his possession whereas there having been no evidence as to how the bank came into possession of the suit property, ought to have held that the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit property ever since it was derequisitioned on 8-1-1947 and the present proceeding being for recovery of possession the burden of proof was on the bank, the plaintiff, to prove its possession and the bank having failed to adduce any evidence in this regard the defendant No. 1 was not required to adduce any evidence of possession and in this state of affairs, when the preponderance of evidence regarding possession was heavily in favour of the defendant No. 1, the learned Single Judge ignoring the preponderance of evidence, wrongly found that the defendant No. 1 was not in possession of the suit property prior to 1955. Further, the finding of the learned Single Judge that Aparna Charan did not take settlement of the entire CS plot No. 1748 and that Sarada Kripa Lala was in possession of the suit property at the time of RS operation and that the defendant No. 1 failed to rebut the presumption of the RS record of rights and the defendant No. 1 went into possession of the suit property taking advantage of the moribund condition of the bank are all contrary to the evidence on record and are the result of surmise and conjecture. It also appears that the learned Single Judge fell in error in relying on Exhibit AA, alleged traced copy of the CS map, to hold that CS Plot No. 1748 was subdivided before RS Operation, inasmuch as Exhibit AA is only a traced copy and there is no evidence on record to show that any competent authority passed any order to treat Exhibit AA as an original CS map and specially when it does not satisfy the requirement of section 83 of the Evidence Act and further, the High Court Division also fell in error in not taking into consideration the judgment and order passed in Civil Appeal No. 16 of 1979 as being not inter parties without considering that the said judgment and order, though not inter parties, was admissible under section 13 of the Evidence Act to prove the fact that the relevant original CS map along with a traced copy was filed in that suit and no division or Bata-dags were shown in the original CS map while such division was shown in the traced copy.
